questions.prompt: A service does 10,000 reads per second. With a 95% cache hit rate, how many reads per second reach the database?
questions.explanation: Only misses reach the database: 5% of 10,000 = 500 reads per second.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, what does the application do on a cache miss?

options.text: Return an error and wait for the cache to load the data
Read from the database, return it, and store it in the cache
Write the value to the database again

questions.explanation: The application owns cache-aside: on a miss it reads the source, then fills the cache for future reads.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of a write-back (write-behind) cache?

options.text: Recent writes can be lost if the cache fails before flushing them to the database

questions.explanation: Write-back acknowledges writes once they're in the cache. If the cache crashes before flushing, those writes are gone, so use it only where some loss is acceptable.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good candidates for a cache with a few minutes of TTL? Select all that apply.

options.text: A product description page viewed thousands of times a minute
A user's profile and avatar URL
The exact stock count used to confirm a purchase at checkout
The result of an expensive 'top sellers this week' query

questions.explanation: Read-heavy, slowly changing or expensive data caches well. The stock count that decides whether a purchase succeeds must be read from the source of truth.

questions.prompt: A hot key expires and thousands of simultaneous misses overload the database. Which techniques prevent this? Select all that apply.

options.text: Request coalescing: one request rebuilds the value while others wait or get the stale value
Refreshing hot entries slightly before they expire
Lowering the TTL on the hot key to 1 second

questions.explanation: Coalescing, early refresh and jitter all stop many requests from rebuilding the same value at once. A shorter TTL makes expiry, and so stampedes, more frequent.
